clue.text: When American heads of urban areas legislate in the typical manner

blocks.note: 'as' can mean 'when', as in 'as I left'
US is the standard abbreviation for American
the opening letter of each of these three words

explanation.surface: American city mayors pass laws in their customary way.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a scene of US city leaders making laws; 'heads' is not mayors but the first letters of three words.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means following the normal routine, exactly what someone would ordinarily expect to happen.

clue.text: Catches rising carbon with the Italian template

explanation.walkthrough: 'The Italian' asks for the Italian word for 'the', a common crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A stencil is a cut-out sheet used as a guide pattern for painting or lettering shapes repeatedly.

clue.text: Man suffering with amazing stress to achieve style

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: Both 'suffering' and 'amazing' signal the rearrangement; the fodder is the two plain words beside them.
explanation.definitionFit: Smartness is the quality of being neatly and fashionably dressed, a close synonym of elegant style.

clue.text: Confused a vacant drunkard and went in front

indicators.note: a vacant thing is emptied of its contents, leaving only the outside letters

blocks.note: taken as written
the outside letters of the word
to lead is to go in front

explanation.surface: A befuddled, glassy-eyed drunk staggers to the front of the queue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vacant' sounds like a blank expression on the drunkard's face but means emptying the word.
explanation.definitionFit: An addled mind is muddled and unable to think clearly, so the adjective matches bewildered.

clue.text: Blessed one and Bartland are seized by crack militant

indicators.note: whatever is seized is gripped and held inside, so these letters sit within another word

blocks.note: a crack is a hole or gap
a saint is a blessed one, abbreviated ST
the setter's name stands for the setter, who refers to themselves as I

explanation.surface: A saint and the setter are captured by an aggressive crack unit.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often name themselves in clues to mean I or ME. 'Crack militant' reads as an elite fighter, but 'crack' is a gap and 'militant' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe someone combative and aggressively opposed, ready to fight rather than cooperate.

clue.text: Numbers racket discovered in spoken exams

indicators.note: something discovered in a place was found sitting inside it, so one word lies within another

a racket is a loud noise, a din

explanation.surface: An illegal numbers racket is uncovered during oral examinations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Numbers racket' reads as an illegal lottery, but the words split: 'Numbers' is the definition and 'racket' means noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinals are numbers expressing position in a sequence, such as first, second and third.

clue.text: Plod quietly alongside streetcar

indicators.note: placed alongside means set next to, so two pieces are simply joined side by side

blocks.note: a streetcar is the American name for a tram
p (piano) is the musical marking for quietly

explanation.surface: Someone trudges silently beside a tram on the street.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue order puts the quiet letter first, but it is placed after the vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: To tramp is to walk heavily and wearily, the same trudging motion as plodding along.

clue.text: Another US canal breaks

indicators.note: another version of something is a different form of it, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Yet another American canal has burst its banks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaks' looks like a verb for the canal bursting, but it is a plural noun meaning gaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacunas are gaps or missing portions, especially in a manuscript or a sequence, so they are interruptions.

clue.text: Average, as this solution is?

blocks.note: surface reading: an expression for ordinary, middle of the road, neither one extreme nor the other
setter's reading: this entry is a down light placed in the central column of the grid

explanation.walkthrough: The entry sits in the centre column of the grid, so it literally runs from top to bottom through its centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Splitting something this way divides it evenly, so the phrase suggests a fair, mean or average position.

clue.text: Prize found in overturned storage compartment

indicators.note: something overturned is flipped end over end, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: a drawer is a sliding storage compartment in furniture

explanation.surface: A prize turns up inside an upturned drawer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found in' might suggest a hidden word, but it simply links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A reward is something given in recognition of an achievement, much like a prize won.

clue.text: Break-dancer on arms

indicators.note: to break something is to smash it apart so the letters can be reassembled differently

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A breakdancer balancing on their arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break-dancer' reads as one word, but the hyphen hides an instruction to break up the letters that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordnance means military weapons, ammunition and artillery, the sense of arms as weaponry.

clue.text: How do cows vocalise depression?

definitions.note: the verb cows perform, not a description of how

blocks.note: first meaning: cattle make a mooing sound
second meaning: a downcast state

explanation.surface: A whimsical question about how cattle express their sadness.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks how cows voice a gloomy mood; the answer is both their mooing verb and a word for gloom.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattle are said to low when they moo, and feeling low or a weather low is depression.

clue.text: Finally gains pyrrhic victory with the reaper's tool

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only each word's closing letter is kept

blocks.note: the closing letter of each of these three words
taken as written

explanation.surface: Death, the Grim Reaper, ends up winning a costly victory with his blade.
explanation.walkthrough: A pyrrhic victory is one won at ruinous cost. 'The' is used as it stands, not as an article.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grim Reaper, a figure of Death, is pictured carrying a long curved blade for cutting crops.

clue.text: Northern Ireland meets Netherlands' openers with awkward spin — they're bowled over!

definitions.note: a plural pronoun phrase standing for the plural noun

indicators.note: openers are what come first, so only the leading letters are taken
something awkward is clumsy and out of place, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: NI is the standard abbreviation for Northern Ireland
an operation, not an abbreviation: the opening pair of letters is taken from the start of the country's name
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket match between Northern Ireland and the Netherlands, where tricky spin bowling skittles the opening batsmen.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket setting makes 'bowled over' sound like batsmen out; it is the pins in a skittles game. Openers are the first batsmen in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Ninepins is a skittles game whose wooden pins are knocked down by a rolled ball.

clue.text: More mature tree

blocks.note: first meaning: older, of greater age
second meaning: a small tree bearing dark berries and white flowers

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an older tree, but the two halves are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative adjective means older, and the noun names a shrubby tree whose berries make cordials.

clue.text: The woman will search for oysters, maybe

blocks.note: she will contracts to she'll
to fish for something is to search for it

explanation.surface: A woman sets off to hunt for oysters, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in the contraction is dropped. 'Search for' looks like a phrase, but 'for' belongs with the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Oysters are one example of hard-cased sea creatures eaten as seafood, hence 'maybe'.

clue.text: Butcher fixed room for kitchen equipment

indicators.note: to butcher something is to chop it up and mangle it, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A butcher has a dedicated room set aside for kitchen appliances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butcher' looks like a person who owns the room; it is a verb telling you to chop up the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A food mixer is an electric appliance for beating and blending ingredients when cooking.

clue.text: Perfect beau lost game

indicators.note: a game leg is a lame or injured one, so the letters are put out of shape

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An ideal boyfriend loses a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like a noun for the match the beau lost, but in the old sense of crippled it signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe something complete and total, as in an absolute or perfect stranger.

clue.text: Poke in the bottom leads to smack — that's a cold response!

blocks.note: to goose someone is to prod them playfully on the bottom
a smack is a knock or bump

explanation.surface: A cheeky prod on the behind earns a slap, and a frosty reaction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold response' seems to mean an unfriendly reaction to the prod; it is literal, the skin reacting to chill.
explanation.definitionFit: A goosebump is a small raised bump on the skin produced when someone feels chilly or frightened.

clue.text: Six balls bound to go too far

blocks.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled
to bound is to leap along, to run

explanation.surface: Six balls are certain to fly too far.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is six deliveries by one bowler. 'Bound' looks like 'certain', but it is a verb for moving fast.
explanation.definitionFit: To overrun is to exceed a limit, such as a time slot or a boundary, so it means exceeding.

clue.text: It detects its echo on substrata or foundations

definitions.note: a clause standing for the noun naming the device

indicators.note: a foundation is what something rests on at its far end, so only the final letters are kept

blocks.note: the closing letter of each of these five words

explanation.surface: A device picks up echoes bouncing back from layers of rock beneath it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites reading 'It detects its echo' as the whole definition; but 'its echo on substrata or' are the five words whose final letters are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonar is a system that locates underwater objects by sending sound pulses and listening for returning echoes.

clue.text: Possibly a disastrous recital

indicators.note: something disastrous has gone badly wrong, so its letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A performance that may well have been a total flop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly a' reads like the start of a hedge about the recital; it is the definition, the word 'a' being one example.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar 'a' is the indefinite article, so it is one instance of this part of speech.

clue.text: Freeholder of the old Arabian sultanate

blocks.note: ye is an old spelling of 'the', as in Ye Olde Shoppe

explanation.surface: A landowner from a former Arabian kingdom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' seems to describe the sultanate, but it belongs with 'the' to give the archaic form.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically a yeoman was an English farmer who owned and cultivated a small estate of land outright.

clue.text: It floats: but if it can't be dumped, it might have to be carried

definitions.note: a clause standing for the noun

definitions.text: if it can't be dumped, it might have to be carried
definitions.note: a clause standing for the noun

blocks.clueFragment: if it can't be dumped, it might have to be carried
blocks.note: second meaning: unproductive staff a team cannot get rid of and so must support

explanation.walkthrough: The first part is literal fallen timber, which floats; the second is the figurative sense of unproductive people that a team ends up carrying.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both dried-out branches and people or things that are no longer useful to an organisation.

clue.text: Put on alternative for patron

blocks.note: to don clothes is to put them on

explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on' suggests staging or pretending; it means dressing in something.
explanation.definitionFit: A donor gives money to support a cause or institution, as a patron of the arts does.

taken as written
taken as written

clue.text: Unruffled Sumatran quilt stuffing

clue.text: Ten mice scurrying around old land of the Aztecs
